header:
Buy now, pay later:
the business model

lines.text: Pay in four is zero interest. So who's paying for it?
lines.say: Pay in four is zero interest. So who's paying for it?

lines.text: Split a $400 order into four, and the store can hand the lender about $10.
lines.say: Split a four hundred dollar order into four, and the store can hand the lender about ten dollars.

lines.text: And for one of the biggest US names in this business, store fees aren't even the main money.
lines.say: And for one of the biggest US names in this business, store fees aren't even the main money.

lines.text: In fiscal 2026, Affirm earned about 48% of its revenue from interest.
lines.say: In fiscal twenty twenty-six, Affirm earned about forty-eight percent of its revenue from interest.

lines.text: So interest-free is only part of the story. There's a store paying, a loan earning interest, and sometimes a late fee.
lines.say: So interest-free is only part of the story. There's a store paying, a loan earning interest, and sometimes a late fee.

lines.text: And this isn't a niche. 16% of US adults used buy now, pay later in 2025, according to the Federal Reserve.
lines.say: And this isn't a niche. Sixteen percent of US adults used buy now, pay later in twenty twenty-five, according to the Federal Reserve.

lines.text: Of those users, 26%, about one in four, paid late at least once that year.
lines.say: Of those users, twenty-six percent, about one in four, paid late at least once that year.

lines.text: So let's open the machine: who pays, how lenders earn, and what it can cost you.
lines.say: So let's open the machine: who pays, how lenders earn, and what it can cost you.

lines.text: Chapter 1: what pay in four really is.
lines.say: Chapter one: what pay in four really is.

lines.text: The classic product is called pay in four. You split one purchase into four equal payments.
lines.say: The classic product is called pay in four. You split one purchase into four equal payments.

lines.text: Take a $400 jacket. The first $100 is due right at checkout.
lines.say: Take a four hundred dollar jacket. The first hundred dollars is due right at checkout.

lines.text: Then another $100 at week two, and another at week four.
lines.say: Then another hundred dollars at week two, and another at week four.

lines.text: The last one lands at week six. Total paid: $400. Interest: zero. That's how the CFPB describes the standard product.
lines.say: The last one lands at week six. Total paid, four hundred dollars. Interest, zero. That's how the C F P B describes the standard product.

lines.text: There's a second kind, too: longer monthly loans that can stretch for months or even years.
lines.say: There's a second kind, too: longer monthly loans that can stretch for months or even years.

lines.text: Those can charge interest. At Affirm, the APR runs from 0% up to 36%.
lines.say: Those can charge interest. At Affirm, the A P R runs from zero up to thirty-six percent.

lines.text: How big is all this? Congress's research service estimates pay-in-four loans reached about $63 billion in 2025.
lines.say: How big is all this? Congress's research service estimates pay in four loans reached about sixty-three billion dollars in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: That sounds massive, but it's only about 1% of the $6.3 trillion Americans put on credit cards that year.
lines.say: That sounds massive, but it's only about one percent of the six point three trillion dollars Americans put on credit cards that year.

lines.text: A small slice that's growing fast. And to see how it pays, we need to follow one $400 order.
lines.say: A small slice that's growing fast. And to see how it pays, we need to follow one four hundred dollar order.

lines.text: Chapter 2: the store pays first.
lines.say: Chapter two: the store pays first.

lines.text: Here's the part shoppers never see. When you pick pay later, the store pays the lender a fee.
lines.say: Here's the part shoppers never see. When you pick pay later, the store pays the lender a fee.

lines.text: It's called a merchant discount fee: a cut of every sale.
lines.say: It's called a merchant discount fee: a cut of every sale.

lines.text: The CFPB studied big lenders and found the average fee was about 3.4% in 2019.
lines.say: The C F P B studied big lenders and found the average fee was about three point four percent in twenty nineteen.

lines.text: By 2021 it had slipped to about 2.5%, as more lenders competed for the same stores.
lines.say: By twenty twenty-one it had slipped to about two and a half percent, as more lenders competed for the same stores.

lines.text: Other estimates run higher. A 2026 report from the advocacy group Protect Borrowers says many lenders charge stores up to 6%, plus about 30 cents.
lines.say: Other estimates run higher. A twenty twenty-six report from the advocacy group Protect Borrowers says many lenders charge stores up to six percent, plus about thirty cents.

lines.text: So let's do our math on the $400 order with the CFPB's 2.49% average. That's $9.96.
lines.say: So let's do our math on the four hundred dollar order with the C F P B's two point four nine percent average. That's nine dollars and ninety-six cents.

lines.text: You pay the full $400. The store gets $390.04. The lender keeps the difference.
lines.say: You pay the full four hundred dollars. The store gets three hundred ninety dollars and four cents. The lender keeps the difference.

lines.text: After your $100 down payment, the lender is owed $300 for up to six weeks.
lines.say: After your hundred dollar down payment, the lender is owed three hundred dollars for up to six weeks.

lines.text: $9.96 on $300 is about 3.3% for six weeks of waiting. That's our math, and it's paid by the store, not you.
lines.say: Nine ninety-six on three hundred is about three point three percent, for six weeks of waiting. That's our math, and it's paid by the store, not you.

lines.text: And if the fee were 6% instead, the same order would cost the store $24.
lines.say: And if the fee were six percent instead, the same order would cost the store twenty-four dollars.

lines.text: So why would any store agree to pay more than it pays for a credit card? Because it can mean more sales.
lines.say: So why would any store agree to pay more than it pays for a credit card? Because it can mean more sales.

lines.text: Richmond Fed researchers put it simply.
lines.say: Richmond Fed researchers put it simply.

scene.text: The fact that merchants are willing to pay such fees suggests that merchants benefit from accepting BNPL.

lines.text: Their point: stores wouldn't pay those fees if it didn't pay off for them.
lines.say: Their point: stores wouldn't pay those fees if it didn't pay off for them.

scene.text: The fact that merchants are willing to pay such fees suggests that merchants benefit from accepting BNPL.

lines.text: That's the pitch lenders make to stores: bigger carts, more finished checkouts, and new shoppers.
lines.say: That's the pitch lenders make to stores: bigger carts, more finished checkouts, and new shoppers.

lines.text: At Affirm, store fees brought in about $1.15 billion in fiscal 2026, the year that ended June 30.
lines.say: At Affirm, store fees brought in about one point one five billion dollars in fiscal twenty twenty-six, the year that ended June thirtieth.

lines.text: That's about 2.3% of the $50.2 billion people spent through Affirm that year, by our math. Close to the CFPB average.
lines.say: That's about two point three percent of the fifty point two billion dollars people spent through Affirm that year, by our math. Close to the C F P B average.

lines.text: But here's the twist. Store fees were only about 27% of Affirm's revenue.
lines.say: But here's the twist. Store fees were only about twenty-seven percent of Affirm's revenue.

lines.text: Chapter 3: the interest engine.
lines.say: Chapter three: the interest engine.

lines.text: Affirm's total revenue in fiscal 2026 was about $4.26 billion. So where did the rest come from?
lines.say: Affirm's total revenue in fiscal twenty twenty-six was about four point two six billion dollars. So where did the rest come from?

lines.text: About 48%, roughly $2.05 billion, was interest on loans.
lines.say: About forty-eight percent, roughly two point oh five billion dollars, was interest on loans.

lines.text: About 27% was the store fees we just did the math on.
lines.say: About twenty-seven percent was the store fees we just did the math on.

lines.text: And the other 25% came from card network fees, selling loans to investors, and servicing those loans.
lines.say: And the other twenty-five percent came from card network fees, selling loans to investors, and servicing those loans.

lines.text: How does a 0% brand earn that much interest? Look at what people borrowed.
lines.say: How does a zero percent brand earn that much interest? Look at what people borrowed.

lines.text: In fiscal 2026, about 70% of Affirm's volume was interest-bearing monthly loans.
lines.say: In fiscal twenty twenty-six, about seventy percent of Affirm's volume was interest-bearing monthly loans.

lines.text: The rest, about 30%, was zero-percent monthly plans and classic pay in four, which Affirm calls Pay in X.
lines.say: The rest, about thirty percent, was zero percent monthly plans and classic pay in four, which Affirm calls Pay in X.

lines.text: Here's what interest looks like on one loan. Say $1,000 over 12 months at 15% APR, a made-up example inside Affirm's range.
lines.say: Here's what interest looks like on one loan. Say one thousand dollars over twelve months at fifteen percent A P R, a made-up example inside Affirm's range.

lines.text: The payment works out to $90.26 a month.
lines.say: The payment works out to ninety dollars and twenty-six cents a month.

lines.text: Over the year you pay back $1,083.10, so $83.10 of that is interest, and it goes to the lender.
lines.say: Over the year you pay back one thousand eighty-three dollars and ten cents, so eighty-three dollars and ten cents of that is interest, and it goes to the lender.

lines.text: Now multiply that across millions of shoppers.
lines.say: Now multiply that across millions of shoppers.

lines.text: Here's how much shopping has flowed through Affirm each fiscal year, from 2019 to 2026.
lines.say: Here's how much shopping has flowed through Affirm each fiscal year, from twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: In fiscal 2019, it was about $2.6 billion.
lines.say: In fiscal twenty nineteen, it was about two point six billion dollars.

lines.text: By fiscal 2022, it had grown to $15.5 billion.
lines.say: By fiscal twenty twenty-two, it had grown to fifteen and a half billion.

lines.text: And in fiscal 2026, $50.2 billion. That's about 19 times bigger in seven years, by our math.
lines.say: And in fiscal twenty twenty-six, fifty point two billion. That's about nineteen times bigger in seven years, by our math.

lines.text: It kept climbing. In the July-to-September quarter of 2026, volume rose 34% to $14.4 billion.
lines.say: It kept climbing. In the July to September quarter of twenty twenty-six, volume rose thirty-four percent to fourteen point four billion dollars.

lines.text: In that quarter, interest income was about $658 million, a little over half of its $1.26 billion in revenue.
lines.say: In that quarter, interest income was about six hundred fifty-eight million dollars, a little over half of its one point two six billion in revenue.

lines.text: So the brand people know for interest-free checkouts is, by revenue, largely a lending business.
lines.say: So the brand people know for interest-free checkouts is, by revenue, largely a lending business.

lines.text: Chapter 4: late fees and Klarna.
lines.say: Chapter four: late fees and Klarna.

lines.text: Pipe number three is late fees. Affirm says it doesn't charge them. Many other lenders do.
lines.say: Pipe number three is late fees. Affirm says it doesn't charge them. Many other lenders do.

lines.text: In CFPB data for 2023, 4.1% of pay-in-four loans got hit with a late fee.
lines.say: In C F P B data for twenty twenty-three, four point one percent of pay in four loans got hit with a late fee.

lines.text: The lenders in that data charged about $136 million in late fees that year, but collected only about $80 million.
lines.say: The lenders in that data charged about a hundred thirty-six million dollars in late fees that year, but collected only about eighty million.

lines.text: Notice something? One average late fee, about $10, is about the same as the whole store fee on our $400 order.
lines.say: Notice something? One average late fee, about ten dollars, is about the same as the whole store fee on our four hundred dollar order.

lines.text: Still, with only a few percent of loans charged, late fees are a side pipe, not the main one.
lines.say: Still, with only a few percent of loans charged, late fees are a side pipe, not the main one.

lines.text: Now the other giant. Klarna, a Swedish company, listed on the New York Stock Exchange in September 2025.
lines.say: Now the other giant. Klarna, a Swedish company, listed on the New York Stock Exchange in September twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: It priced its shares at $40, above its planned range, valuing the company at about $15 billion.
lines.say: It priced its shares at forty dollars, above its planned range, valuing the company at about fifteen billion dollars.

lines.text: Back in 2021, private investors had valued Klarna at $45.6 billion. A year later, it was $6.7 billion.
lines.say: Back in twenty twenty-one, private investors had valued Klarna at forty-five point six billion dollars. A year later, it was six point seven billion.

lines.text: In 2025, shoppers spent about $128 billion through Klarna, and its revenue was about $3.5 billion.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, shoppers spent about a hundred twenty-eight billion dollars through Klarna, and its revenue was about three and a half billion.

lines.text: Klarna's mix is nearly the reverse. About 71% of its 2025 revenue came from transaction and service fees, mostly paid by stores.
lines.say: Klarna's mix is nearly the reverse. About seventy-one percent of its twenty twenty-five revenue came from transaction and service fees, mostly paid by stores.

lines.text: Interest was about 27% of Klarna's revenue, roughly the same share that store fees were at Affirm.
lines.say: Interest was about twenty-seven percent of Klarna's revenue, roughly the same share that store fees were at Affirm.

lines.text: Growth doesn't guarantee profit. Klarna posted a net loss of $273 million in 2025.
lines.say: Growth doesn't guarantee profit. Klarna posted a net loss of two hundred seventy-three million dollars in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: Revenue kept growing: in the April-to-June quarter of 2026, it was $1.04 billion, up 27% in a year.
lines.say: Revenue kept growing: in the April to June quarter of twenty twenty-six, it was one point oh four billion dollars, up twenty-seven percent in a year.

lines.text: So: two giants, two recipes. One leans on interest. The other leans on store fees.
lines.say: So: two giants, two recipes. One leans on interest. The other leans on store fees.

lines.text: Chapter 5: the risks and the rules.
lines.say: Chapter five: the risks and the rules.

lines.text: So what does this mean for the person paying? Pay in four works as promised, until it doesn't.
lines.say: So what does this mean for the person paying? Pay in four works as promised, until it doesn't.

lines.text: Use keeps creeping up: from 10% of US adults in 2021 to 16% in 2025, in the Fed's yearly survey.
lines.say: Use keeps creeping up: from ten percent of US adults in twenty twenty-one to sixteen percent in twenty twenty-five, in the Fed's yearly survey.

lines.text: And late payments rose faster: 18% of users paid late in 2023, and 26% in 2025.
lines.say: And late payments rose faster: eighteen percent of users paid late in twenty twenty-three, and twenty-six percent in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: In 2025, 11% of users said a BNPL payment triggered an overdraft or a bounced-payment fee at their bank.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, eleven percent of users said a buy now, pay later payment triggered an overdraft or a bounced-payment fee at their bank.

lines.text: Private surveys find even more. In a LendingTree survey from March 2026, 47% of users said they paid late in the past year.
lines.say: Private surveys find even more. In a LendingTree survey from March twenty twenty-six, forty-seven percent of users said they paid late in the past year.

lines.text: Most of those were no more than about a week late. But in both surveys, the share is up from two years earlier.
lines.say: Most of those were no more than about a week late. But in both surveys, the share is up from two years earlier.

lines.text: The bigger risk is stacking: several small loans at once, from different apps.
lines.say: The bigger risk is stacking: several small loans at once, from different apps.

lines.text: Each one looks tiny, like $100 here and $75 there. Together, they can crowd the same paycheck.
lines.say: Each one looks tiny, like a hundred dollars here and seventy-five there. Together, they can crowd the same paycheck.

lines.text: And other lenders often can't see them. Congress's researchers say most providers don't consistently report pay-in-four loans to credit bureaus.
lines.say: And other lenders often can't see them. Congress's researchers say most providers don't consistently report pay in four loans to credit bureaus.

lines.text: The report says only one major firm reports all of them. Affirm says it now reports all its loans to Experian.
lines.say: The report says only one major firm reports all of them. Affirm says it now reports all its loans to Experian.

lines.text: Scoring is catching up. In June 2025, FICO announced its first credit scores built to include BNPL data.
lines.say: Scoring is catching up. In June twenty twenty-five, FICO announced its first credit scores built to include buy now, pay later data.

lines.text: With scores like that, paying on time could help a score, and paying late could hurt it, once lenders use them.
lines.say: With scores like that, paying on time could help a score, and paying late could hurt it, once lenders use them.

lines.text: The federal rules have swung, too. In May 2024, the CFPB said pay-in-four lenders should follow credit card rules under the Truth in Lending law.
lines.say: The federal rules have swung, too. In May twenty twenty-four, the C F P B said pay in four lenders should follow credit card rules under the Truth in Lending law.

lines.text: That meant card-style rights, like disputing a charge and getting refunds credited back.
lines.say: That meant card-style rights, like disputing a charge and getting refunds credited back.

lines.text: Then, in May 2025, the CFPB withdrew that rule, along with other guidance documents.
lines.say: Then, in May twenty twenty-five, the C F P B withdrew that rule, along with other guidance documents.

lines.text: A month later, it said it wouldn't reissue it, because a change that big should go through a full public rulemaking.
lines.say: A month later, it said it wouldn't reissue it, because a change that big should go through a full public rulemaking.

lines.text: Supporters said the rule gave shoppers clear protections. The industry called it the wrong process and a poor fit.
lines.say: Supporters said the rule gave shoppers clear protections. The industry called it the wrong process and a poor fit.

lines.text: Some states are stepping in. New York passed a law in 2025 that requires BNPL lenders to get a license.
lines.say: Some states are stepping in. New York passed a law in twenty twenty-five that requires buy now, pay later lenders to get a license.

lines.text: Chapter 6: the recap.
lines.say: Chapter six: the recap.

lines.text: Recap. Pipe one: the store pays a fee, about $10 on a $400 order at the CFPB's 2021 average.
lines.say: Recap. Pipe one: the store pays a fee, about ten dollars on a four hundred dollar order at the C F P B's twenty twenty-one average.

lines.text: Pipe two: interest on longer loans. That was about 48% of Affirm's fiscal 2026 revenue.
lines.say: Pipe two: interest on longer loans. That was about forty-eight percent of Affirm's fiscal twenty twenty-six revenue.

lines.text: Pipe three: late fees, where lenders charge them, about $10 on average in the CFPB's 2023 data.
lines.say: Pipe three: late fees, where lenders charge them, about ten dollars on average in the C F P B's twenty twenty-three data.

lines.text: For the shopper, classic pay in four costs no interest when every payment lands on time.
lines.say: For the shopper, classic pay in four costs no interest when every payment lands on time.

lines.text: The costs show up in four places: interest on longer loans, late fees, overdrafts, and stacking.
lines.say: The costs show up in four places: interest on longer loans, late fees, overdrafts, and stacking.

post.title: Pay in four is 0% interest. So how do Affirm and Klarna make billions?
post.ig: Pay in four is interest-free. So who pays? On a $400 order, the store can pay the lender about $10.
post.tiktok: Pay in four is zero interest. So who's paying for it? On a $400 order, about $10 comes from the store.
post.yt_desc:
Buy now, pay later is sold as zero interest, so how do lenders make billions? This video follows a $400 pay-in-four order to show the merchant fee stores pay (our math uses the CFPB's 2.49% average from 2021), then shows why Affirm earned about 48% of its fiscal 2026 revenue from interest, how Klarna's mix differs, and what late fees really add. We also cover late payments and overdrafts in the Fed's 2025 survey, credit reporting and FICO's BNPL scores, and how the CFPB's 2024 rule was withdrawn in 2025.

CHAPTERS

Sources: Affirm Form 10-K, fiscal year ended June 30, 2026, and fiscal Q1 2027 results (Nov 5, 2026); Affirm S-1 (2020) and 10-Ks (GMV history); Klarna full-year 2025 results (Feb 26, 2026) and Q2 2026 results (Aug 2026); Klarna IPO coverage, American Banker (Sept 2025); CFPB, Buy Now, Pay Later: Market Trends and Consumer Impacts (Sept 2022) and BNPL market report (Dec 2025); Congressional Research Service, R48858 (Feb 18, 2026); Federal Reserve, Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 (May 2026); Richmond Fed Economic Brief 25-03 (2025); Protect Borrowers BNPL report (2026); Affirm/Experian credit reporting release (March 2025); LendingTree BNPL survey (March 2026); FICO (June 23, 2025); Federal Register 90 FR 20084 (May 12, 2025).

News and education, not financial advice.
